# DRAFT — Noise2Noise denoising of mandated ASL repetitions outperforms averaging at the reference noise level

*Draft generated by `experiments/_abstract.py` from the cross-validated results; every number is computed from the result files. Single subject — see Limitations.*

## Synopsis

ASL protocols acquire repeated control–label pairs and average them. We use those mandated repetitions as Noise2Noise training data — no clean reference — and denoise each repetition to the noise level of a leave-one-out reference. Under slice-wise cross-validation, a single denoised repetition is as accurate as the plain average of 6.8 repetitions, and at every averaging depth the approach beats both plain averaging and a Gaussian filter matched to the same residual noise.

## Introduction

Averaging N repetitions reduces noise variance only as 1/N. Deep denoisers usually need clean targets, which do not exist for ASL. Noise2Noise (N2N) needs only independent noisy realizations of the same object — exactly what an ASL protocol already acquires.

## Methods

- **Data:** complex ASL difference images, 34 slices × 10 repetitions, 80 × 80.
- **Model:** a 2-channel (Re/Im) U-Net score model trained per repetition with the leave-one-out mean of the other 9 as target. The network is conditioned on the **total** noise level √(σ_y² + σ_add²), with σ_y estimated per slice from the repetition spread, correcting a common mislabelling of the noise level in diffusion-based N2N.
- **Decoding:** one deterministic DDIM step from the input noise σ to r·σ, `out = x̂0 + r (y − x̂0)`. We lock r = 1/3, the noise of the leave-one-out training target, so every output carries the reference noise level.
- **Validation:** 5-fold cross-validation over slices; each slice scored only by a model that never saw it. Error against the unknown clean map is estimated without bias by splitting each slice's repetitions into an estimation set A and an independent reference set B and subtracting B's known noise variance; accuracy is reported as n_eff = σ²/MSE, the number of plainly averaged repetitions with equal error. Endpoints were pre-registered.
- **Baselines:** plain averaging; a Gaussian filter whose width gives the same residual noise.

## Results

- **Calibration:** achieved residual noise 0.348 of the input (median) for r = 1/3.
- **Single repetition:** n_eff 6.84 — as accurate as a plain average of 6.8 repetitions (better than one raw repetition on 34/34 slices) and 1.062× the noise-matched filter (32/34, p = 3e-09).
- **Averaging denoised repetitions:** with 9, n_eff 34.7 — 3.85× plain averaging (34/34) and 1.187× the noise-matched filter (33/34).
- **Spectral check (single maps):** against the matched filter the network is more accurate in the three lower spatial-frequency bands on every slice; its finest-band error is almost entirely the deliberately kept reference-level noise.
- **Loss and ratio:** the ranking of training losses depends on r; at r = 1/3 unweighted MSE is worse than L1 for single maps (0.951×), while noise-normalized MSE leads when averaging (1.040× at 9). The full posterior mean (r = 0) minimises single-map error but blurs, and over-smooths when many outputs are averaged (n_eff 31.1 vs 34.7 at r = 1/3, 9 repetitions).
- **Robustness:** with r = 0, the pre-registered primary endpoint (5 repetitions) gave 5.96× plain averaging (95% CI 5.23–6.85; 34/34; p = 5.8e-11).

## Discussion and conclusion

Mandated ASL repetitions are sufficient to train a denoiser that, at the reference noise level, outperforms both averaging and noise-matched filtering, with its advantage at coarse and intermediate spatial scales. The decoding ratio is a first-class parameter: it trades residual noise against blur and must be fixed before comparing models.

**Limitations.** One subject and acquisition; Gaussian filtering is the only classical baseline (non-local / BM3D-type filters not yet compared); the model fails on slices quieter than its training data; error-based metrics only (no perfusion quantification yet).

**Future work.** Under independent Gaussian noise the mean of all repetitions is a sufficient statistic, so denoising the mean once is optimal in principle and avoids the shared blur of averaging per-repetition outputs. Training such a model needs many more images at the deployment noise level than one subject provides; the per-repetition approach used here is the practical choice under limited training data. Multi-subject data and target-free training at the deployment noise (e.g. SURE) are the next steps.
